beats.headline: Why does a fast producer crash your JVM?
beats.subline: Classic Observer patterns lack backpressure, leading to OOM errors under heavy load.
beats.narration: Classic Observer patterns are great for UI, but they fail at scale. If your producer emits 50k events per second and your consumer only handles 1k, your memory will explode. Reactive Streams fixes this.

beats.title: Observer vs. Reactive Streams
beats.narration: Classic observers just push data blindly. Reactive Streams adds terminal signals for completion and errors, plus a Subscription channel that lets the consumer request only what it can handle.

beats.title: The Reactive Signal Protocol
beats.subtitle: How demand controls the data flow
beats.narration: The handshake is strict. First, the subscriber gets a subscription. Then, it calls request(n). Only then does the publisher send items. This pull-push mechanism is the heart of backpressure.

beats.title: Manual Backpressure Control

steps.explanation: Explicitly tells the publisher how much data we are ready to process.
We only request more once the current batch is finished.

beats.narration: You rarely write this manually, but it shows the power. By requesting fixed batches, you prevent the producer from overwhelming your system. Next, we look at Mono and Flux.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
takeaways: request(n) is the key to flow control

beats.narration: You've got the theory. In Part 2, we dive into Project Reactor's Mono and Flux, and why your pipeline won't run until you subscribe.

beats.headline: Why is your reactive code doing nothing?
beats.subline: Reactive pipelines are lazy blueprints. They don't execute until you subscribe.
beats.narration: You wrote a complex reactive pipeline, but no database call fired. Why? Because reactive pipelines are just blueprints. Nothing happens until you call subscribe.

beats.title: Mono vs. Flux
beats.narration: Mono is for single results, like a database lookup. Flux is for streams, like a Kafka feed. Both are publishers, but their intent is different.

beats.title: Assembly vs. Execution

steps.explanation: Constructing the operator chain. No logic runs here.
Subscribe triggers the upstream flow and demand.

beats.narration: The assembly phase is just configuration. The execution phase only starts when subscribe is called. If you forget to subscribe, your code is effectively dead.

beats.title: Handling Overflow
beats.caption: What happens when the producer is too fast?

lines.text: # Choose your strategy based on business needs

beats.narration: When you can't slow the producer, use overflow strategies. Drop items, keep only the latest for telemetry, or buffer them. Choose wisely to avoid OOM.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
takeaways: Pipelines are lazy; subscribe() triggers execution
Use backpressure operators for hot sources

beats.narration: Assembly is just the start. In Part 3, we master Schedulers to ensure your event-loop threads never block.

beats.headline: One blocking call can freeze your entire server.
beats.subline: Blocking an event-loop thread is the cardinal sin of reactive programming.
beats.narration: Reactive systems rely on non-blocking threads. If you call a blocking JDBC driver on an event-loop thread, you freeze every other request on that thread. Don't do it.

beats.title: Threading Control
beats.subtitle: Where does the code run?
beats.narration: Use subscribeOn to control the source thread. Use publishOn to switch threads mid-pipeline. This keeps your heavy processing off the main event loop.

beats.title: Offloading Blocking Calls

steps.explanation: Wraps blocking logic into a reactive Mono.
Offloads blocking work to a separate thread pool.

beats.narration: Always use boundedElastic for legacy blocking code. It prevents your reactive event loop from stalling, keeping your application responsive under high concurrency.

beats.title: Scheduler Selection
beats.narration: Use parallel for CPU-heavy tasks. Use boundedElastic for I/O. Mixing these up is the most common cause of performance degradation in reactive systems.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Reactive vs Virtual Threads →
beats.narration: Threading is hard, but essential. In the final part, we compare reactive programming with Java 21's new Virtual Threads.

beats.headline: Are Virtual Threads killing Reactive Programming?
beats.subline: Java 21 changed the game. Here is when you still need WebFlux.
beats.narration: With Java 21 Virtual Threads, you can write simple, blocking code that scales. Does this make Reactive Programming obsolete? Not exactly.

beats.title: Virtual Threads vs. Reactive
beats.narration: Virtual threads win for standard REST APIs. But if you need complex stream processing, windowing, or strict backpressure, Reactive is still the king.

beats.title: When to Choose Which
beats.subtitle: The decision matrix
beats.narration: Choose Virtual Threads for CRUD and request-response. Choose Reactive for WebSockets, Kafka, and telemetry where you need rich temporal operators.

beats.title: Final Verdict
beats.caption: The modern stack choice

lines.text: # Use the right tool for the stream

beats.narration: Don't force Reactive if you don't need it. But don't abandon it if you're building high-performance event-driven pipelines. Both have their place in modern Java.
